cards.text: Isaiah, the LORD's prophet, has the word of the LORD for the scoffers who rule the people in Jerusalem. Here's what they've been saying: "We have made a covenant with death; we have fashioned an agreement with Sheol." Out of EVERYBODY in the world to sign a deal with, they picked DEATH.

cards.question: The rulers in Jerusalem say they've made a deal with death and Sheol. What do they think it gets them?

answers.text: The scourge will not touch them

cards.text: Then they say what their safety rests on, right out loud: "because we have made lies our refuge and falsehood our hiding place." Friend, that's putting tape over the check engine light and calling the car FIXED.
So the Lord GOD answers them. But before He says a word about their hiding place, He talks about a stone He's laying.

cards.question: The Lord GOD is speaking to the rulers in Jerusalem. He says He's laying a stone in ___.
The Lord GOD calls His stone a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation. He says the one who believes will never be shaken.

cards.text: Hold on to this stone, friend. Peter quotes this very line in his first letter and points it to Jesus (1 Peter 2:4-7).
Then the Lord GOD says, "I will make justice the measuring line and righteousness the level." When God holds a level up to your wall, there is no "eh, close enough."

cards.question: The rulers are hiding in a refuge of lies, and a storm is coming for it. What does the Lord GOD say will sweep it away?
The Lord GOD says the rulers' covenant with death will still stand when trouble comes.
The rulers were sure the overwhelming scourge would pass them by. The Lord GOD says that when it passes through, they will be ___ by it.

cards.text: And it won't come just once. It will carry them away, sweeping through morning after morning, by day and by night, and Isaiah says understanding this message will bring sheer terror.

cards.question: Right after that, Isaiah gives a quick picture from everyday life. What is it?

answers.text: A bed too short and a blanket too small
A roof with holes and a door that won't shut
A lamp with no oil and a jar with a crack

cards.text: "the bed is too short to stretch out on, and the blanket too small to wrap around you." Friend, I spent years in a junk drawer under a pile of old paper, and NOT ONE takeout menu ever covered my whole mustache.

Then Isaiah says the LORD will rise up as at Mount Perazim and rouse Himself as in the Valley of Gibeon. At Baal-perazim the LORD burst out against David's enemies like a bursting flood (2 Samuel 5:20), and at Gibeon He threw Israel's enemies into confusion (Joshua 10:10).

cards.question: Isaiah says the LORD will rise up to do His work, and he calls it His strange work.
Isaiah warns the scoffers to stop mocking. If they don't, what does he say will happen to their shackles?
Isaiah has heard a decree of destruction from the Lord GOD of Hosts. It's against the whole ___.

cards.text: Now Isaiah says, "Listen and hear my voice. Pay attention and hear what I say." And then the prophet does something nobody saw coming: he starts talking about FARMING.

cards.question: Isaiah asks, "Does the plowman plow for planting every day?" Does he just keep loosening the soil forever? What answer is Isaiah after?

answers.text: No once it's level he plants
Yes he plows all year long

cards.text: A baker who mixes dough all day and never bakes isn't a baker, friend. He's just a stamper with a VERY tired mustache, and the farmer knows better, so once the ground is leveled, he plants.

cards.question: Isaiah says the farmer throws his wheat, barley and rye all together into one big pile of seed.
Caraway and cumin scattered, wheat in rows, barley in plots, rye within its border. Isaiah says the farmer knows how because his ___ instructs and teaches him properly.

cards.text: Then comes the harvest. Isaiah says caraway is not threshed with a sledge, and a cart wheel is not rolled over the cumin.

cards.question: The farmer doesn't use a threshing sledge on his caraway. What does he beat it out with instead?

cards.text: A stick for the caraway and a rod for the cumin. Different seed, different tool, the same way you don't press a delicate sugar cookie with a sledgehammer, and believe me, I've watched bakers TRY.

cards.question: Isaiah says grain for bread is threshed over and over until the horses crush it.

cards.text: Right. Grain for bread must be ground, but it is not endlessly threshed, and though the cart wheels roll over it, the horses do not crush it.

cards.question: Isaiah wraps up the farming picture. Where does he say all this also comes from?

cards.text: Isaiah says the LORD of Hosts is "wonderful in counsel and excellent in wisdom." Friend, the God who taught that farmer when to stop plowing is NOT winging it.

findings.problem: The passage opens with "Therefore," which points back to verses 7-13 (drunken priests and prophets scoffing at God's message). The opening card doesn't say why the word of the LORD is coming to these scoffers now, so the baker starts mid-thought with no context.

rule.text: The opening card can be up to 3 sentences. It says who is speaking, to whom, and what is going on. If the passage starts in the middle of a thought, it gives the context.

findings.problem: The question says "a storm is coming for it," which points straight to hail and rules out fire and locusts before the baker picks. Verse 17 never says "storm."

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: Nothing on the earlier cards lets the baker reason toward the bed and blanket picture. All three pictures are equally likely, so the right pick comes down to luck. Several other choice cards in this stop are also discovery questions (cards 5, 18), so this one should get more context or ask something else.

rule.text: Before each choice card, Papa Dorin's story card gives enough context that the baker can reason their way to the answer.

findings.problem: This card quotes verse 20 again right after card 13 asked about it. Apart from the joke, it adds nothing and doesn't move the passage forward.

rule.text:
Every story card moves the baker forward through the passage.
- No recap cards.

findings.problem: Isaiah 28:21 doesn't say which events at Perazim and Gibeon it means. The card ties the Valley of Gibeon to Joshua 10:10, but Gibeon also fits David's victory over the Philistines (1 Chronicles 14:16), which sits right alongside Perazim. The card settles a connection the text leaves open. It also packs three beats (the LORD rising up, the Perazim backstory and the Gibeon backstory) into one card.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: This true/false card only checks whether Isaiah used the word "strange." The baker hasn't seen that wording and can't reason it out, so it tests wording, not meaning or movement.

rule.text: Ask about the movement and the meaning: what changes, what the picture is, why the speaker says what he says.

findings.problem: The wrong answer "Only until the rain comes" also means the plowman doesn't plow every day. A baker could argue it's close to the right answer.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: The joke blends the baker image with the farmer in the same line ("and the farmer knows better, so once the ground is leveled, he plants"). The punchline is also confusing: a baker who never bakes turns into "a stamper with a VERY tired mustache." The card mostly repeats card 2's answer.

rule.text: One image only. Never blend the comparison with the Bible setting.

findings.problem: "Believe me, I've watched bakers TRY" makes bakers, the user's own role, the target of the joke instead of Papa Dorin himself.

rule.text: Humble. When a joke needs someone to laugh at, it's himself.

findings.problem: Stop 2 tells the farming picture (verses 23-29) but never asks what it means or why Isaiah tells it after the warning of judgment in stop 1. The baker may leave without seeing how the two halves of the passage connect. The text itself never states the connection.
findings.question: prep-walkthrough.md says to ask "why the speaker says what he says," but the Scripture rules say not to add reasons or connections the text doesn't state. Should Prep connect the farmer picture back to God's measured judgment, or ask about its meaning at all, when Isaiah leaves that link unstated?
